football_evidence.question: Can Colorado’s pass rush get to Jake Fette?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Arizona State, and its own breakdown accounts for about 0.9 of the 5.2 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Arizona State has the ball (big plays on the ground): Arizona State’s offense turns 9.0% of its runs into explosive gains, and Colorado’s defense gives up explosive gains on 6.5% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.5%).

When Colorado has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Colorado’s offense has allowed a sack on 6.1% of its dropbacks, and Arizona State’s defense sacks the quarterback on 6.8% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).
In his last two games (Northwestern and Baylor), Lewis averaged 5.2 yards per attempt, against 9.8 in his two games before that.
EdgeDesk’s position-group ratings put Arizona State’s running backs No. 44 nationally and Colorado’s No. 121.
contradicting: When Arizona State has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Arizona State’s offense has allowed a sack on 8.0% of its dropbacks, and Colorado’s defense sacks the quarterback on 8.7% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).

When Arizona State has the ball (the red zone): Arizona State’s offense succeeds on 31.1% of its red-zone plays, and Colorado’s defense allows success on 36.8% of opponent red-zone plays (FBS average 43.5%).

When Arizona State has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Arizona State’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 18.8% of its runs, and Colorado’s defense stops 22.4% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.5%).
In his last two games (Oklahoma State and Kansas State), Wilson averaged 9.9 yards per attempt, against 6.8 in his four games before that.

Julian Lewis has completed 58 of 93 passes (62.4%) for 709 yards, 7.6 yards per attempt, 6 touchdowns and 2 interceptions in four games for Colorado, and has been sacked on 8 of 101 dropbacks.
